name: inchi
why: Turning molecules into canonical text strings is a real chemistry idea worth an afternoon, though the library itself is fairly plain.

brief.what_it_is: InChI is an open-source structure-based chemical identifier, developed by IUPAC and the InChI Trust. It takes a chemical structure, described by its atoms, bond connectivity, tautomeric, isotope, stereochemistry and charge information, and produces a textual InChI string with those information layers. The README also describes a hashed 27-character InChIKey derived from the InChI, intended for compact storage and search. The repository ships the inchi-1 command-line executable and a C library (libinchi) with the inchi_main demo program. The README's MOLfile and SDfile references suggest molecule files are a main input, but it does not spell out the full input and output workflow.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames InChI as a standard identifier for chemical databases that facilitates information management across chemistry. It says the identifiers are strictly unique, non-proprietary and freely accessible, and that they enable linking chemistry on the web, advancing the FAIR data principles by improving findability and interoperability.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes InChI as layered: the connectivity layer comes first, then tautomeric, isotope, stereochemistry and charge information, each as a separate part of the string. The InChIKey is the hashed, fixed-length form of the InChI. Beta options such as EnhancedStereochemistry rewrite the stereo layers from MOLfile V3000 stereo collections (STEABS, STEREL, STERAC), and the README says those collections are ignored without that option. The README gives no further internal algorithm detail.

brief.install_notes: No account or runtime is needed to use the release binaries. The release archive release_artifacts.zip at github.com/IUPAC-InChI/InChI/releases/latest holds 64-bit builds for Windows, Linux and macOS, containing the inchi-1 executable and the libinchi library with inchi_main. To build from source you need CMake (interactive build tool or CLI), Microsoft Visual Studio projects on Windows, or a Make build with GCC or Clang/LLVM. On Linux and macOS, if libinchi.so or the dylib is not found at run time, set LD_LIBRARY_PATH (or DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH on macOS) as the README describes. Optional bounds-checking functions need a third-party C11 Annex K library, and oneTBB is optional.
brief.standout: The InChI string is designed to be canonical and strictly unique, and the README presents it as an open standard with fuzzing (OSS-Fuzz) and static analysis (Coverity) run continuously. The 27-character InChIKey is a compact hashed form of the same identity, which is what most databases use for lookup.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub README shows a 'Maintained? yes' badge, a CI build badge and a link to the release workflow, and the InChI Trust homepage lists news dated April, June and August 2026, including a planned July 2026 technical meeting. I did not check the release page, so the date of the latest release is unknown.
brief.caveats: Beta features (EnhancedStereochemistry, MolecularInorganics) produce strings that the README says are not stable across releases, so they should not be stored as persistent identifiers. Many experimental options (KET, 15T, PT_* tautomerism flags, Polymers105, InChI2Struct, InChI2InChI and others) are flagged as possibly not functioning and should be avoided. The 32-bit MSVC build has known issues with the AMI options. Pre-C99 C compiler support is being phased out from version 1.07.5. Intel icc is no longer supported. The README contradicts itself on the build helper's name (cmake_build_tool.sh versus inchi_build_tool.sh). The homepage itself contains no technical description, so the project's own text is the GitHub README.
quotes: InChI is a structure-based textual identifier, strictly unique, non-proprietary, open source, and freely accessible.
With its fixed length of 27 characters the InChIKey — the hashed version of the InChI — allows for a compact representation and usage in databases or search engines.
InChI and InChIKey are open standards. They use unique machine readable strings to represent, store and search chemical structures.
